item.title: REVIEW: You asked how Kindle Colorsoft colors look in Dark Mode? The answer might surprise you
item.description:
Source: Latest from TechRadar US in News
On my recent unboxing of the brand-new Kindle Colorsoft Signature Edition (the one with the brushed aluminum back), I noticed someone asking about the quality of colors in dark mode, and I realized I didn't have a good answer. Dark Mode, which became popular on modern screens over the past 15 years or so — a throwback to the original CRT displays — has never been my thing. As a result, I don't use it on phones, browsers, or Kindle e-readers. Still, the more I thought about this question (below). The more I wondered about it. "This might be a dumb question," started one TikTok commenter, "but do the colors still show when in Dark Mode? I've only seen photos in light mode." I instantly tried to imagine what a comic or graphic novel might look like in Dark Mode and realized I'd never seen it that way either. The Kindle Colorsoft shares a menu system with the rest of the monochrome Kindles, with the Dark Mode option sitting right up top. You access the quick menu with a swipe down from the top of the display. You can also dig into settings to turn on the control from there. I turned on Dark Mode on the Kindle Colorsoft Signature Edition and noticed that my library immediately reversed, turning all the white borders black, but the book, magazine, and graphic novel covers remained untouched. If I opened a book, I saw white text on black pages. The other thing I noticed is that the screen looked a lot dimmer. Basically, Dark Mode automatically lowers the screen brightness by half. I opened a graphic novel. As with the rest of the Colosoft interface, the borders around each graphic novel page were black. However, each page was still white, with the untouched color panels inside. Honestly, this makes sense, since I can't imagine any artist would want dark mode reversing their work. It would probably look terrible. I could see all the colors, but the pages looked too dim. Fortunately, I could still push the front-lit LEDs brighter (I turned them up to max) to return some of that vibrancy, though I'm not sure if that defeats the purpose of Dark Mode. The other option is to take advantage of the Kindle Colorsoft's reflective display (unlike an LCD, there are no traditional backlights). If you have a good external light or even sunlight, the page looks great with or without dark mode, which can reduce eye-straining screen glare and save some battery life (not much of an issue with Kindles). Here's what I learned: Yes, you can still see colors in Dark Mode, but as Amazon confirmed to me, "When setting Colorsoft devices to dark mode, the screen may appear dimmer overall due to the color E-Ink layer." If the screen looks too dim, adjust the brightness or find a good light source and enjoy your colorful graphic novels.

item.title: REVIEW: Dell 14S (DS14270) Review: It's Best if You Buy the $649 Base Model
item.description:
Source: PCMag
With ongoing memory shortages driving up laptop prices up and down the market, Dell provides a counterweight with its new 14S. Starting at $649 (also the price of our test configuration), this 14-inch budget laptop uses Intel's "Wildcat Lake" processor platform to deliver essential performance for students, younger users, and anyone focused on everyday tasks like web browsing and streaming. Impressive battery life and a sleek aluminum design in four colors enhance the notebook's appeal, but the 14S only makes sense in its entry configuration, as Dell’s upgrade options quickly push the system into territory occupied by substantially better laptops. The Dell 14S remains a respectable choice if your budget has a firm ceiling, but Dell's own XPS 13 and the Apple MacBook Neo offer substantially more features for not much more money. Dell's Wildcat Lake-based 14S (not to be confused with the mainstream Dell 14S DS14260) starts at $649 with a six-core Intel Core 5 320 processor, 8GB of memory, and 256GB of storage. At that price, it's a reasonably attractive budget laptop for basic tasks. The problem is that every upgrade severely undermines its value. Moving to 16GB of memory also requires stepping up to an Intel Core 7 350 processor and Wi-Fi 6E, adding an eye-watering $450 and raising the price to $1,099. That's well outside budget-laptop territory. Storage upgrades are similarly difficult to justify, with moving to 512GB adding $100 and to 1TB adding $300. Even Dell's display upgrade, which brings a sharper 2,880-by-1,800 panel with a 120Hz refresh rate (our test unit has a 60Hz screen), costs an additional $100. If you're looking to upgrade after purchase, note that the storage drive is removable, but the memory is soldered. All told, the 14S is only a good value in its base configuration; once you add any of these options, its budget-laptop appeal disappears almost immediately. The 14S looks and feels more expensive than its price suggests. Its three-piece aluminum construction is a welcome departure from the plastic fare common among budget laptops, offering a quality feel and impressive rigidity. Dell's four colorways add personality: Linen (our test model), Dusty Rose, Washed Denim, and Velvet Green. A couple of the other colors are shown here alongside our test model. Measuring 0.53 inches thick and weighing 2.53 pounds, the 14S is well-suited for commuting or moving around the house. Though it's not the lightest machine this size, it remains comfortably portable. The XPS 13 is lighter at 2.2 pounds, while the MacBook Neo weighs 2.7 pounds, despite using a smaller display. The port selection is less impressive. The 14S includes two 10Gbps USB-C ports, an HDMI output, and an audio jack, but it omits any classic USB Type-A. That's an inconvenient decision on any laptop, particularly a budget model where buyers are likely to resent spending extra on adapters. The HDMI port is also limited to version 1.4, restricting 4K output to a choppy 24Hz. The system's wireless connectivity is limited to Wi-Fi 6 and Bluetooth 5.3. That's adequate for everyday use, but it reinforces that this laptop is built to hit a price target. The 14S also lacks biometric security features. The 14S's visuals are hard to fault: a 1,920-by-1,200 IPS display provides a sharp image, wide viewing angles, and a practical anti-glare finish. The screen has ample brightness for sunlit rooms and reasonably vibrant colors. Although the panel lacks touch support and is limited to a 60Hz refresh rate, neither omission is a deal-breaker on a budget model. As noted, the optional 2,880-by-1,800 display upgrade seems appealing, but it's hardly sensible when Dell's own XPS 13 offers a similar screen and numerous other advantages for not much more money. Dell's spacious, well-designed touchpad and surprisingly sharp 1080p webcam also exceed expectations in this tier, but the same can't be said about the keyboard and speakers. The speakers sound thin and lack both volume and bass, but the keyboard is the larger disappointment. Its keys have a somewhat cheap texture and an overly plasticky feel, and the lack of backlighting is difficult to ignore. Together, they serve as a persistent reminder that although the 14S looks premium, its budget roots are firmly planted. I tested the base 14S, a system featuring a Core 5 320 processor (six cores, 4.6GHz turbo boost), integrated Intel Graphics, 8GB of LPDDR5X memory running at 7,467MHz, and a 256GB PCI Express 3.0 storage drive. For performance comparison, our test lineup includes two other Wildcat Lake laptops, the Dell XPS 13 and Lenovo IdeaPad Slim 3i 15, plus the Apple MacBook Neo. I also included the HP OmniBook 5 14 to show how a mainstream laptop performs next to these budget models. Our primary overall benchmark, UL's PCMark 10, puts a system through its paces in productivity apps ranging from web browsing to word processing and spreadsheet work. Its Full System Drive subtest measures a PC's storage throughput. Three more tests we rely on are CPU-centric or processor-intensive: Maxon's Cinebench 2024 uses that company's Cinema 4D engine to render a complex scene; Primate Labs' Geekbench 6.3 Pro simulates popular apps ranging from PDF rendering and speech recognition to machine learning; and we see how long it takes the HandBrake 1.8 video transcoder to convert a 12-minute clip from 4K to 1080p resolution. Finally, workstation maker Puget Systems' PugetBench for Creators rates a PC's image-editing prowess through a variety of automated operations in the seminal photo editor Adobe Photoshop 25. The 14S performed reasonably well in PCMark 10, demonstrating enough performance for web browsing, office apps, and streaming. In day-to-day use, it didn't feel slower than the considerably more capable systems I use. But that test alone doesn't reveal the real issue: 8GB of memory simply isn't enough for much else on Windows 11. That limitation surfaced in our other tests. The 14S was unable to complete Cinebench and ran out of memory during our Photoshop benchmark, highlighting how little headroom exists. I observed more than 80% of its memory in use while it was idle, let alone with any apps running. The Core 5 320 is reasonably capable; it generally matched the XPS 13 and MacBook Neo in the tests the 14S could complete, but no amount of CPU power will overcome the lack of memory. The 256GB PCIe 3.0 storage drive also highlights the bare-bones nature of this laptop, with an underwhelming PCMark 10 storage score. However, its impact on everyday performance won't be as noticeable as that of the 8GB of memory. In terms of Handbrake performance, the 14S fell in the middle of the pack, a little more than 3 minutes behind the OmniBook 5 14's 6-minute-and-43-second mark. We challenge all systems' graphics with a quintet of animations or gaming simulations from UL's 3DMark test suite. The first two, Wild Life (1440p) and Wild Life Extreme (4K), use the Vulkan graphics API to measure GPU speeds. The next pair, Steel Nomad's regular and Light subtests, focuses on APIs more commonly used for game development to assess gaming geometry and particle effects. Last up, we turn to 3DMark Solar Bay to measure ray-tracing performance. The 14S's graphics performance is what you'd expect from an entry-level laptop. Its integrated Intel Graphics solution showed performance on par with the other Wildcat Lake systems, but that's not saying much. Certainly, don't expect to play serious games on this laptop. Several of our benchmarks wouldn't run due to hardware limitations, from a lack of ray tracing support in 3DMark's Solar Bay to insufficient memory for Steel Nomad. We test each laptop and tablet's battery life by playing a locally stored 720p video file (the open-source Blender movie Tears of Steel) with the display brightness set to 50% and the audio volume at 100%. We make sure the battery is fully charged before the test, with Wi-Fi and keyboard backlighting turned off. To gauge display performance, we also use a Datacolor SpyderX Elite monitor calibration sensor and its software to measure a laptop screen's color saturation—what percentage of the sRGB, Adobe RGB, and DCI-P3 color gamuts or palettes the display can show—and its 50% and peak brightness in nits (candelas per square meter). The 14S offers impressive battery life. Lasting 22 hours in our rundown, it outdid the MacBook Neo by several hours and should last a few days of light use between charges. HP's OmniBook proved untouchable, but its time doesn't diminish Dell's achievement in the entry-level laptop space. That sentiment follows into display quality. The 14S's color coverage didn't quite match the XPS 13 or MacBook Neo, but it's solid, and brightness surpassed Dell's own 300-nit rating. Dell 14S (DS14270) - 5.0 - Exemplary: Near perfection, ground-breaking - 4.5 - Outstanding: Best in class, acts as a benchmark for measuring competitors - 4.0 - Excellent: A performance, feature, or value leader in its class, with few shortfalls - 3.5 - Good: Does what the product should do, and does so better than many competitors - 3.0 - Average: Does what the product should do, and sits in the middle of the pack - 2.5 - Fair: We have some reservations, buy with caution - 2.0 - Subpar: We do not recommend, buy with extreme caution - 1.0 - Dismal: Don't even think about buying this product Read Our Editorial Mission Statement and Testing Methodologies. The Dell 14S is easy to like in its $649 base configuration, offering a premium aluminum design, distinctive color options, a surprisingly good display, and all-day battery life at a price where plastic chassis and so-so screens are the norm. Its shortcomings, including a lack of keyboard backlighting and an 8GB memory limit, are tolerable given the price. The problem is that the 14S's value proposition falls apart the moment you start adding options. It only takes one option to push its price to within striking distance of the Dell XPS 13 and Apple MacBook Neo, both of which offer superior displays, stronger overall performance, and more refined features. As a result, the 14S earns a cautious recommendation: if your budget tops out at $649, it's a solid choice, but shoppers who can spend a bit more should skip the upgrades and look at the XPS 13 or the MacBook Neo instead. Computers are my lifelong obsession. I wrote my first laptop review in 2005 for NotebookReview.com, continued with a consistent PC-reviewing gig at Computer Shopper in 2014, and moved to PCMag in 2018. Here, I test and review the latest high-performance laptops and desktops, and sometimes a key core PC component or two. I also review enterprise computing solutions for StorageReview. I work full-time as a technical analyst for a business software and services company. My hobbies are digital photography, fitness, two-stroke engines, and reading. I’m a graduate of the Rochester Institute of Technology.

item.title: REVIEW: Dreame Ecceluxe Go review: a pocket-sized espresso maker with its own boiler for easy coffee at camp
item.description:
Source: Latest from TechRadar US in News
A compact, self-heating espresso machine that takes three different types of coffee pods or fresh grounds, the Dreame Ecceluxe Go is perfect for coffee-lovers on the move. Its cordless design is ideal for off-grid brewing at camp or on hiking trails, and it's small enough to tuck into the pocket of your backpack. Just be careful not to accidentally hit the power button when reaching for it, and be prepared to wait while it gets to temperature. - +Works with three types of coffee capsules, and ground coffee - -Brewing with cold water takes six minutes Why you can trust TechRadar We spend hours testing every product or service we review, so you can be sure you're buying the best. Find out more about how we test. The Dreame Ecceluxe Go is a compact, cordless espresso machine that’s ideal for camping trips, hikes, and any excursions where you don’t have ready access to a stove or kettle. That’s because, unlike most portable coffee makers, the Ecceluxe Go heats the water itself, after which its small but powerful pump extracts your shot of espresso. The brewer itself is smaller than most travel mugs, and comes in a smart carry case with a set of adapters that are compatible with three different types of coffee capsules, plus loose grounds. For the easiest brewing, just insert a Nespresso Original, Nestlé Dolce Gusto, or ESE (Easy Serve Espresso) pod into the appropriate adapter and you’re ready to begin. Brewing with cold water takes about six minutes, and you can brew two or three times on a single charge. If you do have access to hot water, however, you can switch to direct brewing mode, which uses water directly from the water tank, and brews much faster. It’s an excellent and very thoughtfully designed little brewer that’s much more versatile than other portable espresso machines I’ve tested. My only real complaint is that it’s easy to accidentally hit the touch-sensitive control button when handling and setting it up. Dreame has yet to announce a price for the Ecceluxe Go, so I have rated the device based solely on design and performance. I will update this review with a value score when the price is published. Dreame Ecceluxe Go: price and availability - Launching in Spain and Portugal first, followed by the US The Dreame Ecceluxe Go is expected to launch in Spain and Portugal by the end of 2026, although the exact date has yet to be confirmed. It should launch in the US shortly after, but there's no UK or Australian launch planned at the moment. No pricing details are available yet. - Super-compact design, with carry case for attachments - One control button, which cannot be locked The Dreame Ecceluxe Go is roughly the size of a soda can, and comes in a smart cushioned carry case together with a collection of attachments. These include three adapters that allow you to brew using Nespresso Original pods, Nestlé Dolce Gusto capsules, ESE (Easy Serve Espresso) pouches, or ground coffee. There’s also a ring to help reduce mess when adding a dose of ground coffee, and a cup for your brewed espresso. The Ecceluxe Go is charged using a covered USB-C port on the front, and is controlled via a small touch-sensitive LED display that lets you power the machine on, and switch between programs. It’s responsive, and shows all the information you need: battery charge level, brewing program, and temperature. My only criticism is that it’s easy to accidentally press this screen when holding the coffee maker, and there’s no way to lock it to prevent that happening accidentally. A physical power button, or a locking switch would make it perfect. - Two brewing modes: self-heating and direct - Accepts three types of coffee pods, or ground coffee The Dreame Ecceluxe Go is refreshingly simple to use. First, choose the right adapter (they're color-coded, but each one also has a small illustration to make life easier), insert your coffee capsule or grounds, and screw it shut. Then just twist the adapter onto the base of the brewing unit, unfold its two support legs, place it on the plastic coffee cup, and you’re ready to begin. The Ecceluxe Go has two brewing modes: P1, which heats water from room temperature before brewing your coffee, and P2 (direct extraction), which uses water already heated to the correct temperature. Brewing using P1 isn’t quick — it takes six minutes for the Ecceluxe Go to reach its brewing temperature of 203F / 95C, then extract a shot of espresso — but that’s understandable. A machine this compact has a tiny heating element and small battery, and since you’ll be using this mode on the move, you can carry on with other camping or work tasks while it’s working. A loud beep will let you know when your drink is ready, and the Ecceluxe Go will turn itself off automatically when it’s finished. P1 also uses a lot of power, and the battery will be completely drained of charge after two or three brews. Thankfully, the USB-C connector means it’s easy to change indoors or in a car, so it will be ready the next time you need a pick-me-up. If you have access to a kettle, P2 takes a fraction of the time and power, and still yields a nicely extracted shot with a respectable layer of crema. In fact, the Ecceluxe Go would make a great single-serve coffee maker for small apartment or van living. It’s much more compact and versatile than even the smallest Nespresso or Keurig coffee maker, and practically mess-free. The adapters and coffee cup can all be cleaned by hand using warm water, and will air-dry in only a few minutes. I test a lot of coffee makers here at TechRadar, and I’ve become particularly fond of the Ecceluxe Go. It takes all the hassle out of brewing delicious espresso at camp, or even on a break mid-hike. The days of drinking lukewarm coffee from a flask at lunchtime are over. Should you buy the Dreame Ecceluxe Pro? This is the perfect brewer for off-grid adventures. Charge it up, pack a couple of coffee pods, and you can brew up anywhere using water from your drinking bottle. No space for an extra appliance on your counter? The Ecceluxe Go is ideal, particularly if you use its fast direct brewing mode. The Dreame Ecceluxe Go can only hold enough charge to make two or three drinks at a time in its self-heating mode. If you want to prepare drinks for more than a couple of people, you’d be better off with a large camping kettle and an AeroPress XL. The classic AeroPress in a super-portable format that all packs down into a travel cup. You'll need a way to heat your water, and it doesn't accept coffee capsules, but it's a great-quality, affordable way to brew on the move. The Nanopresso is a hand-pumped espresso machine, so there's no need to worry about charging or batteries. There's even an adapter available for Nespresso Original pods, but it can't heat its own water. I used the Dreame Ecceluxe Go for two weeks instead of my usual espresso machine. I tested it with Nespresso Original style capsules (from a local coffee roaster), Nestlé Dolce Gusto pods, Illy ESE pods, and freshly ground coffee beans. I tested the Ecceluxe Go's self-heating and direct extraction modes, timing how long it took to extract a shot of coffee, and monitoring how far the battery charge level dropped after each brew.

item.title: SALES: Flowkey Piano App Offers Discounted Subscriptions for Classical Music Lessons
item.description:
Source: PCWorld, PCMag
The flowkey Piano Learning App is offering discounted subscription plans for users seeking to learn classical piano pieces. A one-year Classic Plan subscription is currently priced at $29.97 (regular price $189), while a five-year plan is available for $59.97 (MSRP $899) through November 1. Both options provide access to over 1,000 classical and public-domain compositions by composers such as Bach, Beethoven, Chopin, Debussy, and others, arranged for Beginner, Intermediate, Advanced, and Pro levels. Lessons include structured practice sessions with interactive feedback, allowing users to identify and correct mistakes in real time. The app listens through a device’s microphone or MIDI connection to flag wrong notes, with features like Wait Mode holding lessons until correct keys are played. Difficult passages can be slowed, looped, or broken into one-hand practice segments to improve accuracy. Expert pianist videos and synchronized sheet music provide visual guidance alongside the music, helping users match fingering with notes. Additional courses cover music theory, chord progressions, sheet music reading, rhythm, and hand coordination. Subscribers can access content across multiple devices, including Windows PCs, Macs, Chromebooks, iPhones, iPads, and Android phones, though mobile devices require iOS 15.6 or Android 11 and later. A digital piano or keyboard is necessary for practice, and lessons are available in 11 languages. Returning players can start at higher skill levels and use included courses to rebuild fundamentals. The promotions expire on November 1 at 11:59 p.m. PT.

item.title: SALES: Halloween food deals 2026: Free meals, discounts and spooky treats
item.description:
Source: NBC 7 San Diego
Halloween can add up fast, from bags of candy for trick-or-treaters to costumes, decorations and plans for the big night. But celebrating doesn’t have to break the bank. From free treats to discounted meals, these Halloween deals can help families save a little money while making the most of Oct. 31. Planning dinner around trick-or-treating? Several restaurants are offering kids-eat-free deals for Halloween, giving families a chance to grab a meal before heading out for candy without stretching the budget. Other promotions include free treats and discounts on family favorites. Offers vary by restaurant, and some require an adult entrée purchase, a rewards membership or a promo code. Check with your local restaurant for availability and restrictions before heading out. Looking for a way to feed the kids before trick-or-treating? These restaurants are offering free or discounted meals for children, often with an adult purchase. Applebee's: Children ages 12 and under in costume can get a free meal when an adult buys an entrée at select locations on Halloween. Chick-fil-A: Individual franchise locations may offer free kids' meals or treats for children in costume, or special catering promotions. Check your local restaurant's website or social media for confirmed Halloween offers. Trump administration's social media posts ahead of elections criticized for being inflammatory Doctor shares 3 lifestyle habits to reduce breast cancer risk Denny's: Kids eat free on Halloween with the purchase of an adult entrée when dining in. The offer is limited to one kids' meal per adult entrée, with a maximum of two kids' meals per ticket. McDonald's: Collectible Disney Villains Boo Buckets featuring Maleficent, Ursula, Cruella de Vil, Jafar and Scar are available with Happy Meals through Oct. 31, while supplies last. MOD Pizza: Kids ages 12 and under who arrive in costume can get a free kids' meal with the purchase of a regular-size pizza or salad on Oct. 31. The offer is for in-restaurant orders. Outback Steakhouse: Get a free kids' meal with the purchase of an adult entrée on Oct. 31. The offer is available for dine-in or online orders with code SPOOKYFREE. Rainforest Cafe: Children ages 10 and under wearing costumes can get a 99-cent kids' meal with each adult entrée purchase through Oct. 30. Guests must mention the offer to their server. Las Vegas and Disney theme park locations are excluded. Red Lobster: From Oct. 30 through Nov. 1, kids dining in costume can get up to two free kids' meals per table with the purchase of a full-price adult dinner entrée. For takeout, use code SPOOKY26 online to get one free kids' meal per adult entrée. Red Robin: Children under 11 wearing costumes can get a free kids' sundae with the purchase of a kids' meal from Oct. 30 through Nov. 1. The offer is dine-in only and limited to one per child. Wendy's: Get a $1 Boo! Book through Nov. 1. The book includes five coupons for free Jr. Frosty treats and one coupon for a $1.99 kids' meal with a purchase. The Frosty coupons remain valid through Dec. 31. Baked by Melissa: Save 20% on any 100-pack of bite-sized cupcakes through Oct. 31 with promo code TRICK20 at online checkout. Purchasing a Hocus Pocus 50-pack also automatically adds a free Boo Crew six-pack to the digital cart. Baskin-Robbins: Rewards members can get 31% off scoops on Oct. 31. Check the Baskin-Robbins app for offer details. Blue Bunny: Get a buy-one-get-one-free deal on frozen dairy desserts when ordering through DashMart on DoorDash from Oct. 29 through Nov. 4. Dairy Queen: The Spellbound Series runs through Nov. 1 and includes the Bubble Brew Sparkler, Enchanted Oreo Blizzard and Ghost Pepper Sauce. A $4 mystery Blizzard Buddy plush keychain is available with any order through Oct. 31, with a chance to find a rare Goldie plush that wins free Blizzards for a year. Edible Arrangements: Save 30% on select Halloween treats through Oct. 31 with code TREAT30 in the Edible app. Seasonal options include the Scary Berry Platter, Spooky Season Fruit Arrangement and Boo Berry Box, with prices starting at $54.99 before the discount. Same-day delivery or pickup is available in eligible areas. Gong cha: Rewards members can get 50% off a second drink when they buy one drink in person at the cashier on Oct. 31. Costumes are encouraged. Jamba: Use promo code SPOOKY for 31% off eligible orders on Halloween. Catering is excluded. Krispy Kreme: Wear a Halloween costume on Oct. 30 or 31 to receive one free Original Glazed or Classic Ring doughnut at participating U.S. shops. No purchase is necessary, and the offer is limited to one doughnut per guest. Marie Callender's: Save on whole bakery pies and cheesecakes when ordering online for pickup throughout October. Savings range from $5 off one item to $40 off six. Nothing Bundt Cakes: The OREO Dirt Cake Bundtlet arrives Oct. 26, featuring chocolate cake, OREO cookie pieces, chocolate pudding filling and a gummy worm topping. Pumpkin Spice Cake is available through Nov. 29. Both are sold in individual Bundtlet sizes. Paris Baguette: PB Rewards members can get a free pastry with any beverage purchase on Oct. 31. 7-Eleven: Save $10 on a 7NOW delivery order of $20 or more on Oct. 31 with promo code TREAT at in-app checkout. Burger King: Royal Perks members can unlock a digital buy-one-get-one Whopper Jr. coupon on Oct. 31 through the BK app or website. The limited-time Vampire's Bite Strawberry & Sprite, featuring an edible Sour Punch candy straw, is also available for $3.59. California Pizza Kitchen: The chain's 7-inch CPKids Jack-O'-Lantern Pizza is available for $5 throughout October for dine-in or takeout. Families can also order a Build Your Own Take & Bake Kit to decorate pizzas at home. Chipotle: The chain's annual Boorito promotion returns on Halloween. Chipotle Rewards members who wear a costume and visit a participating restaurant between 3 p.m. and closing can get a $6 entrée. Guests must scan their rewards card at checkout. The offer is for in-restaurant orders, with one discounted entrée per member. Fresh Brothers: Preorder a pumpkin-shaped pizza for Oct. 31 and use code FBSPK15 to save 15%. The offer is available online or in the app. Hot Dog on a Stick: Through Oct. 31, get a free gallon of Hand-Stomped Lemonade with the purchase of a Party Pack by ordering online and entering code LEMONADE. KFC: Get 50 KFC Nuggets for $20 on Halloween. Check the KFC app or your local restaurant for availability and ordering details. Long John Silver's: From Oct. 30 through Nov. 1, get a Chicken & Mac Party Pack for $15 when ordering online or through the app at participating locations. The meal includes nine pieces of hand-battered, all-white-meat chicken and a family-size mac and cheese topped with Crumblies. item.title: SALES: It’s snow time: the best winter activity holidays in Europe for non-skiers
item.description:
Source: The Guardian Travel
Arctic thrills and survival skills in Finnish Lapland At Ruka, the first skiers of the year slalomed down the slopes on 2 October. Just inside the Arctic Circle, Ruka’s long snow-sure season and cosy village atmosphere make it a popular ski resort with Finnish families. The long polar nights mean there are only a few hours of dim twilight each day, but the slopes here are floodlit, so that never stops play. The Narnia-like setting offers just as much action off the runs as on them, and in December the resort launches Ruka Guides, guided adventures from a dedicated activity centre. Spend the morning e-fatbiking through snowy forests (from €90) or cutting a hole in a frozen lake to catch fish (from €89), before learning Arctic survival skills (from €85) or snowshoeing in the evening darkness on the hunt for the northern lights (from €89). Other, more offbeat diversions include floating in a thermal suit down the freezing Kiveskoski river in meditative silence (from €135), whizzing down an alpine coaster at up to 25mph (from €11.88) and practising your sun salutation in the forest surrounded by grazing reindeer (from €45). Dasher and Dancer are a clue to the other reason Ruka is such a hit with children: the main merry man himself. Father Christmas, Mrs Claus and the elves live at Santa’s Cottage, about 30 minutes’ drive from Ruka, where they test how good little helpers are at gingerbread baking and Christmas card making, before those wannabe elves sing Santa’s favourite carol to him in Finnish, post cards at the post office and sledge down the hillside outside (from €105).
All activities at ruka.fi. Rukariutta Superior apartments sleep up to six from €362 a night (rukapalvelu.fi). Lumo Lakeside Lodges sleep up to two adults and two children from €215 (rukasafaris.fi) In the depths of winter, the sun sets just a shade after 3.30pm in the Cairngorms national park and doesn’t rise again until about 8.50 the following morning. Those long hours of darkness combined with low levels of light pollution (the area around Tomintoul and Glenlivet is an International Dark Sky Park) makes it the perfect place for stargazing. While it’s easy to be dazzled by the Milky Way without even reaching for a telescope, the Discovery Centre in the village of Tomintoul lends out stargazing kits (pre-booking required) to help visitors delve deeper into the cosmos at one of their recommended viewing sites, such as the nearby Tomintoul Field of Hope, with its purpose-built Skyhide pavilion. The centre is also the meeting point for astronomy events (there is a close-up look at the moon on 18 November and an evening of meteor spotting when the Geminids shower is at its peak around mid-December (suggested donation £7, cairngormsdarkskypark.org). A short drive away, just north of Aviemore, storyteller Sarah Hobbs leads monthly Stargazing Storywalks. The 1½-mile after-dark amble weaves in Gaelic and Pictish tales of the night sky from thousands of years ago, from warrior queens to one-eyed giants, and ends with a cup of foraged wild tea (£20pp, Oct-March). For something a little more strenuous, Hillgoers organises regular three-mile night walks with certified star rangers, spotting glowing planets and nocturnal wildlife (£40pp, maximum of eight in a group). The Lazy Duck continues the dark-sky theme with a clutch of off-grid huts among the pines of the Abernethy Forest with stargazing windows above the beds (from £187 a night in December). There are plenty of winter activities in daylight hours too, from driving the SnowRoads route, which winds along the highest public roads in Britain, to meeting the country’s only free-roaming reindeer herd (guided hill trips run Feb-Dec from £29.40pp, cairngormreindeer.co.uk). At the foot of Mont Blanc, Chamonix is famous among skiers for its gnarly off-piste terrain and intense black runs. But that dramatic landscape makes it prime territory for action off the slopes too. One of Responsible Travel’s new trips this season is a four-night self-guided snowshoeing holiday in the Chamonix valley. Using the traditional mountain spa town of Saint-Gervais-les-Bains as its base, the itinerary ventures deep into the snow-covered Vallorcine valley, hiking through larch meadows and pine forests, heading up the Flégère gondola to walk along a balcony trail facing Mont Blanc, and taking in the views from the summit of Mont d’Arbois at 1,833 metres. The Mont Blanc massif is one of the most densely glaciated areas in the Alps, and while the ice is receding due to the climate crisis, taking the dinky red Montenvers cog train up to the Mer de Glace is still an impressive experience. This huge river of ice winds some 5 miles between the mountains, and at the top a cable car followed by around 200 steps descends into the Grotte de Glace, a blue tunnel carved into the glacier (€49.70 for the train, gondola and ice cave visit). A more intrepid ice-spotting option is Les Contamines-Montjoie circular snowshoeing route, which climbs through pine forests to the Plateau du Truc, with its views of the d’Armancette, Miage and Covagnet glaciers. Back in Chamonix, the Mont-Blanc Museum opened in July, tracing the valley’s history and Alpine exploits from the ice age to today, showcasing objects that include memorabilia from the first Winter Olympic Games (held in Chamonix in 1924) and the walking stick of Jacques Balmat, half of the two-man team that made the first ascent of Mont Blanc in 1786. That climb is only for serious mountaineers, but the cable car from Chamonix town centre is a shortcut to Aiguille du Midi’s almost-as-impressive 3,842-metre peak (€43 round trip) – leaving plenty of energy to hit the nearby La Luge toboggan run (€23 for the pedestrian lift pass and one descent; ski-saintgervais.com).
A four-night self-guided snowshoeing trip in Chamonix from £790pp with Responsible Travel, including B&B accommodation, route maps, smartphone navigation app, GPS trackers and 24/7 phone support
Snowshoeing and bear spotting in Transylvania Hiking along narrow trails in the Piatra raiului national park, you’re more likely to come across bear or wolf tracks than other walkers’ footprints. The Carpathian mountains are one of Europe’s last bastions for large predators – there are thought to be more than 10,000 brown bears and around 2,500 grey wolves in Romania alone. A week-long guided trip with Exodus makes tracks into Transylvania’s dramatic karst landscape, and is an atmospheric introduction to snowshoes and crampons. Base camp is the family-run Villa Hermani guesthouse, over 1,000 metres above sea level in the village of Magura, where there’s always a warming glass of homemade pălincă (fruit brandy) waiting. Hikes climb up to the high ridge of Dealul Măgurice or to the plateau between the Piatra Craiului and Bucegi mountains, where the only thing that might break the silence is the howling of a wolf. One of the most spectacular walks heads along the Zărnești Gorge, its vertical limestone walls rising 200 metres above the icy canyon floor. When not snowshoeing through Christmas-card scenes, take in medieval churches, the cobbled old town of Brașov and the Libearty bear sanctuary, which has rescued over 120 brown bears from the cruelty of captivity. And while Bram Stoker never set foot in Romania, let alone Bran Castle (often said to be the inspiration for Dracula’s lair), you can. With its frosty turrets and towers set against the Carpathians, it looks more gothic than ever, and even better without the bloodthirsty summer crowds.
Exodus’s seven-night Transylvania winter walk and snowshoe trip from £1,459pp, including all accommodation, meals, transport and activities, tour guide, snowshoes and poles Igloos and Christmas markets in Innsbruck Innsbruck is ringed by the Austrian Alps, meaning wherever you wander in the city – among the medieval alleys of the Altstadt or past the colourful houses along the River Inn – snow-covered mountains are the constant backdrop. Those jagged peaks are home to 12 ski areas within 15 to 75 minutes of the city by public transport, and some are worth the trip for the snow-plough-averse too. Zaha Hadid’s swooping, modernist Bergisel ski jump is a dominant sight above the town and the vertiginous view is even better from its observation deck. The architect also designed four of the Nordpark Cable Railway stations that feature fluid glass canopies mimicking natural ice formations and glaciers. They take skiers and non-skiers up to the Nordkette mountains for a bird’s eye view of the Tirolean capital. There’s plenty more to get pulses racing without clipping on a pair of skis, from bobsleighing down the 1,399-metre Olympic track at Igls at speeds of up to 115km/h (from €45 for bobrafting, €119 for piloted race bobsleighing) to night sledding at Rangger Köpfl (€25). For more icy fun, there are igloos to spend the night in at Iglu-Dorf in Kühtai, Austria’s highest ski resort (from €537 for up to three people, including cheese fondue, community sauna and breakfast). Back down in Innsbruck, Christmas market season kicks off in November, and there are seven dotted around the streets and squares, from the historic old town market to the lofty Hungerburg – be sure to try kiachl, a doughnut-like pastry served either savoury with hot sauerkraut, or sweet topped with wild cranberry jam. New skating experience Ice Magic also launches this winter, with illuminated ice paths connecting different parts of the city, alongside light installations and projections, ice disco nights and DJs (from €8). While Scandinavians started using animal bones to make primitive ice skates thousands of years ago, wild, or Nordic, skating as we know it (long-distance skating outdoors on natural ice for sport rather than utility) evolved in Sweden in the 1900s. Stockholm’s Skridskoseglarklubb (“Skate Sailing Club”) was formed in 1901 and today has more than 10,000 members, who share the latest ice information online to find the ideal skating locations. Nordic skates have long blades attached only at the front of the boot, used to make long, rhythmic glides; other specialist safety kit includes long, pointy poles to assess ice thickness and a backpack that doubles as a flotation device. Wild is the operative word here, and it is prudent as a beginner to skate with a pro. Stockholm-based Ice Guide runs a number of trips, from one-day introductions to multi-day tours, which head out on to Lake Mälaren or the Baltic Sea in the Stockholm archipelago (from £143 including all gear, transport and lunch). Hellasgården, less than half an hour outside Stockholm, is another popular skate spot with ploughed tracks on Lake Källtorpssjön, and there are holes cut in the ice for the bravest swimmers (and a sauna for after). While in the city centre, get your frozen kicks at the ice rink at Kungsträdgården (skate rental about £7.50 an hour) or by joining the boisterous crowd at a Djurgården IF ice hockey match at the Hovet stadium.
Ruby Frida opened this summer and has doubles from £70 room-only A foodie walk in the Dolomites, northern Italy Hearty Tirolean food is made for winter: Knödel dumplings smothered in melted butter and parmesan, the ricotta- and spinach-filled pasta pockets of Schlutzkrapfen, the cast-iron skillet hash of Bauerngröstl. Hiking through the slopes and valleys of the Dolomites’ Drei Zinnen (Three Peaks) nature park on a week-long trip with self-guided walking holiday specialists Inntravel is a good way to work up an appetite. From the charmingly traditional Hotel Drei Zinnen in the village of Sesto near the Austrian border, a network of 100km of well-groomed, partially cleared paths (meaning no snowshoes required) branches out through the Fischleintal valley and beyond into the nature park. Mountain huts (rifugios) are dotted along routes for a warming lunch: Talschlusshütte serves mountain pine and porcini mushroom risotto and classic comforting Gerstensuppe (barley soup) along the Fischleintal valley walk; while the 100-year-old Dreischusterhütte among the fir trees in the nearby Innerfeldtel valley is much loved for its Kaiserschmarrn (shredded pancake) and homemade Apfelkiachl (fried apple rings). Other routes start with a cable car ride and cut across the snowglobe landscapes of the Kreuzbergpass (stopping for a drink on the terrace at the Klammbach hut, of course) or loop around the banks of the frozen Lake Toblach. Hotel Drei Zinnen has welcomed a fair few winter explorers through its doors since it opened in 1930. One regular guest – the mountaineer and author of Seven Years in Tibet Heinrich Harrer – inspired the hotel’s original owner Hans Watschinger to transform the establishment and the village of Sesto (Sexten in German) into a winter destination. It’s still run by the Watschinger family, and today there’s daily afternoon cake and a Finnish sauna to ease walk-weary muscles, and four-course nightly feasts of Italian favourites and local South Tirolean specialities to fuel up for another day in the mountains.
A seven-night Italian Dolomites Winter Walking trip from £1,076, including half-board accommodation, local bus pass and transfers (inntravel.co.uk) Husky sledding, reindeer and the northern lights in Norway For as long as the lights of the aurora borealis have danced across the sky, the people living beneath them have told stories explaining the mysterious, spectral glow – are they omens or gods, communication from spirits or threat of war? For some Sámi communities in northern Scandinavia, they were the souls of the dead, souls that were not to be disturbed by looking, talking, waving or pointing at them, in case the ghostly veil snatched you into the sky or cut off your head. At 217 miles (350km) above the Arctic Circle, Tromsø is the ideal destination for northern lights chasers and learning about the indigenous Sámi people – many of whom still herd reindeer across the vast wilderness. The Oskal family have lived a way of life shaped by reindeer for generations, and their herd spends winter around the camp near Tromsø and summer roaming free in the mountains. The family now share that traditional way of life through Tromsø Arctic Reindeer, opening up their camp to visitors to sled ride, feed the herd and join the family around the fire in the lavvu (tent), for joik (traditional Sámi song) and perhaps glimpses of the aurora overhead (experiences start at 990 kroner/£75 for reindeer feeding). At the gateway to Norway’s frozen far north, Tromsø is the launchpad for numerous activities – ice fishing and fjord cruising, husky sledding and snowmobile safaris – and the lively university town is interesting in itself. It was once the departure point for expeditions to the north pole – a history captured at the Polar Museum on the harbour front – and today also draws cultural travellers for concerts in the angular Arctic Cathedral and the international film festival in January.
Three-night trip to Tromsø from £767pp, including B&B and an aurora-chasing trip, with Discover the World

item.title: SALES: iPhone Duo vs iPhone 18 Pro: which should you choose?
item.description:
Source: Latest from TechRadar US in News
The iPhone Duo is a phone-and-tablet all-in-one, offering an extra screen at a much higher price than the iPhone 18 Pro. It also loses some key Pro features. The iPhone 18 Pro is a much cheaper phone than the iPhone Duo, with better cameras to boot. But its single screen makes it far less versatile. The iPhone Duo has been a long time coming, but is Apple’s first foldable a home run? And even if it is, do you even really need a dual-screen device? Those are questions you might be asking yourself if you're in the market for a new iPhone — especially when the iPhone 18 Pro is also available, which only has one display but is a better device in various other ways. So, to help you decide which of these two models is best for you, we’ve compared the iPhone Duo and iPhone 18 Pro across various categories, including price, display, and design. Happy decision-making! iPhone Duo vs iPhone 18 Pro: specs comparison Before we look in depth at the key elements of the iPhone Duo and iPhone 18 Pro, the specs table below provides an overview of their similarities and differences. iPhone Duo vs iPhone 18 Pro: price and availability The iPhone Duo and iPhone 18 Pro were both announced in September 2026. But while the iPhone 18 Pro shipped shortly after its announcement, the iPhone Duo wasn’t available until October 23. Both phones are available now, though, across much of the world. The iPhone Duo starts at $1,999 / £1,999 / AU$3,499, for which you’ll get 256GB of storage. There’s also a 512GB model for $2,199 / £2,199 / AU$3,899, a 1TB version for $2,599 / £2,599 / AU$4,699, and a 2TB model for $3,199 / £3,199 / AU$5,899. The iPhone 18 Pro is a lot more affordable (relatively speaking), while still being expensive. This device starts at $1,199 / £1,199 / AU$2,099 for 256GB of storage, rising to $1,399 / £1,399 / AU$2,499 for 512GB, $1,799 / £1,799 / AU$3,299 for 1TB, and $2,399 / £2,399 / AU$4,499 for 2TB. So, the iPhone Duo’s starting price is some $800 / £800 / AU$1,400 higher than the iPhone 18 Pro's; that difference is the price of a high-end phone (or indeed the new iPad mini) all on its own. So while you’re essentially getting a phone and tablet all in one with the Duo, you’re also paying handsomely for that privilege. The iPhone Duo doesn’t really look like any other iPhone, and not just because it folds. When folded shut, you might expect it to look like the iPhone 18 Pro, but you’d be wrong, as it has a much shorter, passport-shaped footprint, coming in at 117.8 x 84.1 x 11.3mm compared to the iPhone 18 Pro’s 150 x 71.9 x 8.8.mm size. Of course, the iPhone Duo is substantially larger when unfolded, opening out to 117.8 x 164.6 x 5.2mm (we'll touch on their displays in the next section). Other differences include the phones' respective camera arrangements. The iPhone Duo has a punch-hole camera in the top right corner of its cover display, and an under-screen camera in its foldable display. The iPhone 18 Pro, meanwhile, has a much larger cut-out for its Dynamic Island, but this larger opening also allows for Face ID, which the iPhone Duo lacks. On the back, the iPhone Duo has a horizontally arranged dual-lens camera, while the iPhone 18 Pro has a larger triple-lens camera block (which Apple describes as the 'camera plateau'). The Duo is also unsurprisingly heavier at 254g to the iPhone 18 Pro’s 211g, and their colors differ, with the iPhone Duo being sold in Night Sky and Star White shades, while the iPhone 18 Pro is available in Black, Silver, Glacier, and Burgundy options. Their materials differ a bit too, with the iPhone Duo having a titanium frame and a glass back (not unlike the iPhone Air), while the iPhone 18 Pro has an aluminum frame and uses a mix of metal and glass on the back. However, both phones have an IP68 rating for dust and water resistance, and both use Ceramic Shield 2 on the front and Ceramic Shield on the back — so they should be similarly durable, aside from the inherent fragility that comes with a second screen and a hinge mechanism (Apple has confirmed to TechRadar that the Duo's viral screen-cracking issue only affected a "small number of units" at launch, so you shouldn't worry about experiencing that level of vulnerability). Ultimately, we praised the designs of both these phones, with our iPhone Duo review describing it as “beautifully designed and engineered,” while our iPhone 18 Pro review highlighted its “fantastic” new shades. There's certainly a learning curve to be experienced with the iPhone Duo's folding form factor — its volume buttons, for instance, are positioned on the top, not the side — while the iPhone 18 Pro feels extremely familiar in the hand. But we'd urge you to try the Duo out for yourself in a store before dismissing its design as a reason not to buy it. In essence, both of these devices are a treat to use. If you’re considering the iPhone Duo, then its screen is probably the most important factor for you, since it has two of them. The Duo's main display is a 7.6-inch 1878 x 2670 foldable LTPO Super Retina XDR OLED panel, with a 120Hz refresh rate, 430 pixels per inch, and a peak brightness of 3,000 nits. The aspect ratio of this inner display is a content-friendly 1.4:1, giving you room to run two full apps side-by-side, play games on a larger canvas, or watch wide-format media (note, though, that most YouTube and Netflix content is still displayed in 16:9). Crucially, this inner screen also features a nano-texture coating to reduce glare and make the Duo's crease appear invisible face-on. Sure, you can see this crease when looking at an angle, but nano-texture really does work for making you forget about the crease during general use. Being a foldable phone, the iPhone Duo also has a 5.4-inch 1398 x 2034 LTPO Super Retina XDR OLED cover screen, which likewise has a 120Hz refresh rate, a peak brightness of 3,000 nits, and around 460 pixels per inch. The iPhone 18 Pro just has one screen, but it’s a good one. It's a 6.3-inch 1206 x 2622 LTPO Super Retina XDR OLED panel with a 120Hz refresh rate, a peak brightness of 3,000 nits, and around 460 pixels per inch. On paper, then, the iPhone Duo’s screen specs are very similar to those of the iPhone 18 Pro — except you get both a bigger and a smaller screen here than the Pro’s mid-size display. But the Duo has an extra trick up its sleeve, as its foldable screen also supports the Apple Pencil, which the iPhone 18 Pro doesn’t. As far as screen quality goes, though, there’s not much to choose between these two devices, with our iPhone Duo review praising its “bright, sharp, fluid screens” along with a surprisingly well-hidden crease, and our iPhone 18 Pro review calling its display “punchy, sharp, and smooth.” While the iPhone Duo arguably has the edge where screens are concerned, it’s the iPhone 18 Pro that takes the win for photography. The Duo has two rear cameras: a 48MP f/1.6 wide snapper and a 48MP f/2.2 ultra-wide with a 120-degree field of view. It also has a decent 12MP f/2.2 camera on the cover screen, and a paltry 4MP f/1.8 under-display camera on the foldable screen. The iPhone 18 Pro, on the other hand, has a triple-lens camera setup on the back, with the same ultra-wide snapper as the Duo, but a superior 48MP variable aperture wide camera that can move between f/1.5 and f/4.0. It also has a 48MP f/2.8 telephoto camera capable of 4x optical zoom. The selfie camera on the iPhone 18 Pro is also slightly higher spec than that of the Duo, being an 18MP f/1.9 one. So, if you buy the Duo, you’ll be getting a less versatile wide camera and no telephoto camera, along with fewer megapixels for its front-facing cameras. Of course, the Duo is far from a bad camera phone, with our review praising its “two strong 48MP lenses and an above-average Center Stage selfie camera.” You can absolutely take great shots with either of these phones. But when it comes to photography, Apple's first foldable is simply no match for the iPhone 18 Pro, which we summed up as offering “better detail” than its predecessor, along with “strong low-light performance, and excellent 4x and 8x zoom.” The iPhone 18 Pro is one of the best camera phones you can buy; the Duo is good, but not great. iPhone Duo vs iPhone 18 Pro: performance and software The iPhone Duo and iPhone 18 Pro should offer comparable performance, as both phones have an A20 Pro chipset, 12GB of RAM, and a vapor chamber. That’s a capable combination, with our iPhone Duo review mentioning “smooth performance across the board,” while our iPhone 18 Pro review highlighted that it’s “fast, efficient, and ready for whatever comes next.” Obviously, the iPhone Duo may be a more enjoyable phone to play mobile games on (given its larger inner screen), but it's not an inherently better or more powerful gaming phone than the iPhone 18 Pro. The same applies to productivity, since you can split the Duo's display in two by swiping up from the bottom and slowly dragging an app left or right. For obvious reasons, you can't do any such multitasking magic on the iPhone 18 Pro. The software on both phones is similar, with the iPhone Duo running iOS 27.1 out of the box and the iPhone 18 Pro running iOS 27. At the time of writing, both phones can be updated to iOS 27.2, and it’s likely they’ll be supported for the same amount of time. There are, however, some software differences to be aware of, with Apple taking advantage of the Duo's dual-screen nature to add and change some features. While using its cover screen, for instance, you'll notice a status bar and side-positioned dock that's easier to reach with your thumb, but sometimes cuts into the Duo's screen real estate. Several apps, too, are not yet optimized for the Duo's unusual screen sizes — first-party apps like Mail and Safari look great, but others (like LinkedIn and Instagram) are a little clunky at the time of writing. These optimization issues will almost certainly be resolved quickly as app developers release Duo-specific updates, but they're worth bearing in mind nonetheless. The iPhone Duo has a 4,883mAh battery, while the iPhone 18 Pro has either a 4,288mAh cell (if you’re getting an eSIM-only model like those sold in the US) or a 4,056mAh cell. So in either case, the iPhone Duo has a higher-capacity battery, but it won’t necessarily last longer, with Apple claiming it can manage an impressive 44 hours of video playback if you're only using the outer display, but just 31 hours if you're mostly using the larger foldable screen. The iPhone 18 Pro, meanwhile, splits the difference at 34 hours. For ‘typical use,’ they’re similar, with the iPhone Duo listed at 24 hours and the iPhone 18 Pro at 23. In our own tests, we found that the iPhone Duo had “solid all-day battery life,” while the iPhone 18 Pro offered “outstanding endurance.” So neither phone should run low on battery too fast. When they do need charging, the iPhone Duo can be juiced to 50% in around 20 minutes with a 60W or higher charger, or it can reach 50% in 30 minutes with a 35W or higher MagSafe charger. The iPhone 18 Pro is slightly faster here, with Apple claiming it can reach 50% in just 15 minutes with a 60W wired charger, and the same 50% in 30 minutes with a 35W MagSafe charger. Those speeds proved accurate in our testing. The iPhone Duo and iPhone 18 Pro are refreshingly different product offerings from Apple. They're similar in some ways, but very distinct in others. The Duo gives you both phone- and tablet-sized screens, along with a higher-capacity battery and stylus support, at a much, much higher price than the iPhone 18 Pro — which itself has better cameras, Face ID, and a slightly faster-charging battery. In other areas, they’re largely similar devices, offering comparable power and software (despite some early teething issues for the Duo), plus similar-quality outer screens. The Duo gets a beautiful nano-texture inner display, though by virtue of it being a foldable phone, it's also heavier than the iPhone 18 Pro, and when folded shut, it’s also thicker. So you’ve really got to think about what factors are most important to you and whether the benefits of the iPhone Duo outweigh its enormous price. Indeed, at such a high cost, you might want to consider buying both the iPhone 18 Pro and an iPad mini instead. Still, the Duo is more pocketable than an iPad (crucially, you're getting two device experiences in one), and it’s an undeniably great phone, scoring 4.5 stars in our review. So if it suits your needs, you’re unlikely to regret buying it. Just be aware of the learning curve.
